content: The following are professional interpretations of the provided references: 1. Ford et al. (2015) discuss the evolving role of CD4 cell count monitoring in the management of antiretroviral therapy (ART), emphasizing its potential future applications in clinical practice. 2. Vojnov and the Clinton Health Access Initiative (2015) evaluate the effectiveness of returning early infant diagnosis (EID) results via SMS/GPRS printers compared to traditional methods for HIV-exposed infants under 18 months. 3. Violari et al. (2008) demonstrate that initiating antiretroviral therapy early significantly reduces mortality rates among HIV-infected infants. 4. The International Community of Women Living with HIV and the Global Network of People Living with HIV (2016) explore the perceptions, values, and preferences of women living with HIV regarding early infant diagnosis in Kenya, Namibia, and Nigeria. 5. Fox and Rosen (2010) systematically review patient retention in ART programs in sub-Saharan Africa, analyzing data from individuals on treatment for up to three years. 6. Rosen and Fox (2011) examine retention rates in HIV care between testing and treatment initiation in sub-Saharan Africa, identifying key challenges and solutions. 7. Penn et al. (2015) systematically review interventions aimed at improving retention in ART programs for HIV-infected individuals in resource-limited settings. 8. Grimwood et al. (2012) highlight the positive impact of community adherence support on retention rates among children receiving ART in South Africa. 9. WHO (2013) provides consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, offering a public health approach to ART delivery. 10. Luque-Fernandez et al. (2013) assess the effectiveness of patient adherence groups as a care model for stable ART patients in Khayelitsha, South Africa. 11. Braitstein et al. (2012) describe a clinician-nurse model that reduces early mortality and improves clinic retention among high-risk HIV patients starting combination ART. 12. Hall et al. (2015) review qualitative evidence on barriers and facilitators to interventions aimed at improving HIV care retention. 13. Geldsetzer and Bärnighausen (2015) systematically review interventions to enhance retention of postpartum women in HIV care. 14. Catalani et al. (2013) systematically review the use of mobile health (mHealth) technologies for HIV treatment and prevention. 15. 16. Beckham et al. (2015) conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to explore gender differences in HIV treatment outcomes, particularly mortality rates. 17. Bangsberg et al. (2001) establish that non-adherence to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) predicts progression to AIDS. 18. Nachega et al. (2007) investigate adherence to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor-based HIV therapy and its virologic outcomes. 19. Wood et al. (2003) analyze the impact of CD4 cell count thresholds on ART outcomes. 20. Mills et al. (2006) systematically review barriers and facilitators to HAART adherence in both developed and developing nations. 21. Martin et al. (2007) identify patient, caregiver, and regimen characteristics associated with adherence to HAART among HIV-infected children and adolescents. 22. Nachega et al. (2012) conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of ART adherence during and after pregnancy across income settings. 23. Colvin et al. (2014) review health system barriers and enablers for ART among HIV-infected pregnant and postpartum women. 24. Hodgson et al. (2014) examine individual and contextual factors influencing ART initiation, adherence, and retention in pregnant and postpartum women. 25. Kim et al. (2014) systematically review and analyze ART adherence among adolescents living with HIV. 26. Murphy et al. (2003) identify barriers to HAART adherence among HIV-infected adolescents. 27. Lowenthal et al. (2014) review challenges faced by adolescents with perinatally acquired HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. 28. Hussen et al. (2015) review the transition of youth living with HIV from pediatric to adult-oriented healthcare. 29. Fetzer et al. (2011) explore barriers and facilitators to pediatric ART adherence in sub-Saharan Africa through a qualitative study. 30. Ivanovska et al. (2014) review challenges and progress in pediatric drug formulations. 31. Bagenda et al. (2011) compare adherence to tablet and liquid formulations of ART in pediatric HIV treatment in Uganda. 32. Uthman et al. (2014) systematically review the relationship between depression and ART adherence across income settings. 33. Gonzalez et al. (2011) conduct a meta-analysis on the impact of depression on HIV treatment non-adherence. 34. Nakimuli-Mpungu et al. (2012) review the effects of depression and alcohol use on ART adherence in sub-Saharan Africa. 35. O’Neil et al. (2012) identify factors associated with ART adherence among HIV-positive adults in British Columbia, Canada. 36. Pyne et al. (2011) evaluate the effectiveness of collaborative care for depression in HIV clinics. 37. Lucas et al. (2006) demonstrate improved HIV treatment outcomes with directly administered ART in methadone clinics. 38. Mountain et al. (2014) systematically review ART uptake, adherence, and outcomes among HIV-infected female sex workers. 39. Graham et al. (2013) assess ART adherence and clinical outcomes among young adults engaging in high-risk sexual behavior in Kenya. 40. Mills et al. (2015) systematically review interventions to enhance ART adherence globally. 41. Cantrell et al. (2008) pilot food supplementation to improve ART adherence among food-insecure adults in Zambia. 42. Munoz et al. (2010) evaluate community-based directly observed therapy for HAART in resource-poor urban settings. 43. Qingyan et al. (2015) systematically review global qualitative evidence on ART adherence interventions. 44. Pangaea Global AIDS Foundation (2015) reports on community-led consultations for WHO’s consolidated treatment guidelines. 45. Bonner et al. (2013) review the use of viral load monitoring to reinforce ART adherence. 46. Court et al. (2014) identify short-term adherence tools predicting ART failure on second-line protease inhibitor-based therapy. 47. Henegar et al. 48. Sangeda et al. (2014) find pharmacy refill adherence outperforms self-reported methods in predicting HIV therapy outcomes. 49. 50. Wu et al. (2014) demonstrate that combining pill count and self-reported adherence predicts first-line ART failure. 51. ART-LINC Collaboration (2008) evaluates ART in resource-limited settings, focusing on patient characteristics and treatment regimens. 52. WHO (2015) provides guidelines for scaling up ART in resource-limited settings. 53. Johnson et al. (2013) analyze life expectancy among South African adults starting ART. 54. Mills et al. (2011) evaluate life expectancy in low-income countries for individuals receiving combination ART. 55. Nsanzimana et al. (2015) study life expectancy among HIV-positive patients in Rwanda. 56. Mills et al. (2006) review barriers and facilitators to HAART adherence globally. 57. Koole et al. (2014) identify retention and risk factors for attrition in ART programs in Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia. 58. Bemelmans et al. (2014) explore community-supported care models for HIV treatment in sub-Saharan Africa. 59. Apollo et al. (2015) analyze the effect of clinic visit frequency and medication pick-up on ART outcomes. 60. Kredo et al. (2014) review task-shifting from doctors to non-doctors for ART initiation and maintenance. 61. WHO (2015) provides recommendations for clinical mentoring to support HIV care scale-up. 62. Kredo et al. (2013) review decentralizing HIV treatment in lowand middle-income countries. 63. Duff et al. (2010) identify barriers to accessing HAART among HIV-positive women in Uganda. 64. Muchedzi et al. (2010) examine factors affecting access to HIV care in Zimbabwe’s PMTCT program. 65. Killam et al. (2010) evaluate ART in antenatal care to increase treatment initiation among HIV-infected pregnant women. 66. Ong’ech et al. (2012) compare service delivery models for HIV-exposed infants. 67. Turan et al. (2012) study the integration of HIV and antenatal care in Kenya. 68. Vo et al. (2012) assess patient satisfaction with integrated HIV and antenatal care services in rural Kenya. 69. Tsague et al. (2010) compare PMTCT service delivery models during the transition to multi-drug ART regimens. 70. Winestone et al. (2012) evaluate the feasibility of integrating HIV care into antenatal clinics in Kenya. 71. WHO (2015) provides recommendations on postnatal care for mothers and newborns. 72. Auld et al. (2015) analyze ART enrollment characteristics and outcomes among HIV-infected adolescents.
